text: Onboarding is the only part of your product experience that a hundred percent of people are ever going to touch. Good luck getting a hundred percent feature adoption of anything else in your product, right?
speaker: Adam Fishman
context: Lenny asks Adam about onboarding as a growth lever and what gets him excited about investing in onboarding optimization. Adam explains why onboarding is such a critical part of the product experience that companies should prioritize. He emphasizes that onboarding is unique because it's the only feature with 100% user adoption, and it's the first chance to deliver on your brand promise to customers.
text_ko: 온보딩(onboarding)은 제품 경험에서 모든 사용자가 한 번쯤은 거치게 되는 유일한 부분이에요. 제품의 다른 어떤 기능도 100% 기능 채택(feature adoption)을 얻기란 거의 불가능해요, 그렇죠?
text_zh: 用户引导(onboarding)是你产品体验中唯一一个百分百用户都会接触到的环节。你产品里其他任何功能想达到百分百的使用率？那基本不可能，对吧？
text_es: La incorporación de usuarios es la única parte de tu producto que el cien por ciento de la gente va a usar sí o sí. A ver si logras que el cien por ciento adopte cualquier otra función de tu producto, ¿no?
key_sentence: Onboarding is the only part of your product experience that a hundred percent of people are ever going to touch.
original_text: Onboarding is the only part of your product experience that a hundred percent of people are ever going to touch. Good luck getting a hundred percent feature adoption of anything else in your product, right? But onboarding is the thing that you have to go through in order to use the product. It's also the first opportunity that you have as a company to deliver on the promise that you made out in the marketplace.

vocabulary.definition: Onboarding refers to the process of integrating new users or employees into a system or organization, ensuring they understand how to use the product or their role effectively.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, onboarding is crucial for user retention and satisfaction, as it sets the foundation for a positive experience with the product or company.
vocabulary.nuance: Onboarding can imply a structured process, and it is often emphasized in customer success strategies to enhance user engagement.

vocabulary.definition: Feature adoption is the process by which users begin to utilize and integrate new features of a product into their regular usage.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech startups, tracking feature adoption is essential for understanding user engagement and the overall success of product updates or new releases.
vocabulary.nuance: Feature adoption can vary widely among users, and low adoption rates may indicate usability issues or a lack of awareness.

text: I like to think of your brand is the promise that you're making and your product experience is your delivery of that promise.
speaker: Adam Fishman
context: Adam continues explaining why onboarding is such a crucial growth lever for companies. He describes the relationship between brand promises and product delivery, emphasizing that these must be perfectly aligned. Adam warns that onboarding is the critical moment where customers first experience whether the product matches their expectations from marketing and sales efforts.
text_ko: 제 생각에는 브랜드(brand)는 고객에게 하는 약속이고, 제품 경험(product experience)은 그 약속을 실제로 지키는 방식이에요.
text_zh: 我觉得品牌就是你对客户的承诺，而产品体验就是你兑现这个承诺的方式。
text_es: Me gusta pensar que tu marca es la promesa que les estás haciendo a tus clientes, y la experiencia con tu producto es cómo cumples esa promesa.
key_sentence: your brand is the promise that you're making and your product experience is your delivery of that promise.
original_text: I like to think of your brand is the promise that you're making and your product experience is your delivery of that promise. And those two things have to be in lockstep with each other, or you're going to have mismatched expectations and some really disappointed customers. So this is the first chance that a customer has to be really excited or really disappointed in what they thought they were getting. So don't mess that up.

vocabulary.definition: Product experience refers to the overall interaction a customer has with a product, encompassing usability, design, and emotional response. It is a critical factor in customer satisfaction and retention.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, optimizing the product experience is vital for user engagement and can differentiate a product in a competitive market.
vocabulary.nuance: This term emphasizes the holistic view of user interaction; it should be used when discussing aspects beyond just functionality, including aesthetics and emotional impact.

vocabulary.definition: Delivery in a business context refers to the process of providing a product or service to the customer, including logistics, timing, and quality of service. It is a critical aspect of fulfilling customer expectations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups and tech companies, effective delivery mechanisms can enhance customer satisfaction and operational efficiency, directly impacting sales and reputation.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply not just physical delivery but also the timely and effective provision of services; it should be used when discussing logistics or service fulfillment.

text: The goal of the competency model is not to find a unicorn human being that is an 11 out of 10 on every one of these things, because frankly, that person doesn't exist.
speaker: Adam Fishman
context: Lenny asks Adam about the components of his growth competency model for hiring growth professionals. Adam explains that the model isn't about finding perfect candidates who excel at everything, but rather about building balanced teams. He emphasizes that even experienced growth executives like himself aren't perfect at all skills, and the key is ensuring your team collectively covers all necessary competencies without gaps.
text_ko: 역량 모델(competency model)의 목적은 이 모든 항목에서 10점 만점에 11점인, 말하자면 '유니콘' 같은 사람을 찾아내는 게 아니에요. 솔직히 그런 사람은 없거든요.
text_zh: 能力模型的目标不是要找到一个十全十美的人，每项能力都超级强，说实话，这样的人根本不存在。
text_es: El objetivo del modelo de competencias no es encontrar a una persona perfecta que sea un 11 de 10 en todas estas áreas, porque seamos realistas, esa persona no existe.
key_sentence: the goal of the competency model is not to find a unicorn human being that is an 11 out of 10 on every one of these things
original_text: The goal of the competency model is not to find a unicorn human being that is an 11 out of 10 on every one of these things, because frankly, that person doesn't exist. I am not an 11 out of 10 on these skills and I have been a growth executive at many companies. I consider myself to be pretty good at the job. The goal is to create a well-rounded team so that you're hiring and balancing skills across your team and that you don't have any gaps in your portfolio.

vocabulary.definition: A competency model is a framework that outlines the skills, knowledge, and behaviors required for effective performance in a specific role or organization.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, competency models are used for recruitment, training, and performance evaluation to ensure alignment between employee capabilities and organizational goals.
vocabulary.nuance: While competency models aim to identify essential traits for success, they should not be viewed as rigid checklists but rather as flexible guidelines that can adapt to individual strengths.

text: One of the challenges of hiring a senior person is that they're all off writing newsletters and making podcast. Not that we know anybody who does that or anything, but... So I don't want to right now go back and work at a company again.
speaker: Adam Fishman
context: Lenny asks whether founders should focus on finding up-and-coming growth talent versus senior executives. Adam humorously points out that many senior growth professionals have moved into advisory roles or content creation, making them unavailable for full-time positions. He suggests that founders shouldn't necessarily want the most senior person anyway when building their first growth function.
text_ko: 시니어를 채용할 때 겪는 문제 중 하나는 다들 뉴스레터(newsletter) 쓰고 팟캐스트(podcast) 만들러 나가 있다는 거예요. 물론 저희가 실제로 그런 사람을 알고 있는 건 절대 아니지만요... 그래서 저는 지금 당장은 다시 회사로 돌아가서 일할 생각은 없어요.
text_zh: 招聘资深人才的一个难点就是，他们现在都在写newsletter(新闻通讯)、做播客去了。我们当然不认识这样的人啦，但是吧...所以我现在也不想再回公司打工了。
text_es: Uno de los problemas de contratar gente senior es que todos andan escribiendo newsletters y haciendo podcasts. No es que conozcamos a nadie que haga eso ni nada, pero... Entonces ahora mismo no me dan ganas de volver a trabajar en una empresa otra vez.
key_sentence: One of the challenges of hiring a senior person is that they're all off writing newsletters and making podcast.
original_text: One of the challenges of hiring a senior person is that they're all off writing newsletters and making podcast. Not that we know anybody who does that or anything, but... So I don't want to right now go back and work at a company again. I'm enjoying what I'm doing and so it's hard to get me, right? But also you don't want me, I think, when you're doing this for the first time.

vocabulary.definition: Difficulties or obstacles that require effort to overcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, challenges often refer to issues that companies face in achieving their goals, such as market competition, resource limitations, or operational inefficiencies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a need for strategic thinking and problem-solving skills to navigate complex situations.

text: So if you're going to hire a junior person, the key is, how do you help them learn? And I think if you don't know what you're doing as the founder or the leader, it's hard.
speaker: Adam Fishman
context: Adam continues discussing the strategy of hiring junior growth talent instead of senior executives. He explains that while hiring junior people can work well, founders need to invest in proper support systems like advisors, education, and mentorship. Adam uses a vivid metaphor to illustrate how enthusiastic but inexperienced people can waste effort on the wrong approaches when they lack proper guidance.
text_ko: 그래서 주니어(junior)를 뽑을 거면 핵심은 어떻게 그들이 배울 수 있도록 도와줄지예요. 그리고 창업자(founder)나 리더(leader)로서 뭘 하는지 모르면 그게 어렵다고 생각해요.
text_zh: 所以如果你要招一个初级员工，关键问题是怎么带他们成长。我觉得如果你作为创始人或者领导自己都不太清楚怎么做，那就很难带好人了。
text_es: Si vas a contratar a alguien junior, lo clave es: ¿cómo lo ayudas a aprender? Y creo que si como fundador o líder no tienes claro lo que haces, se complica todo.
key_sentence: the key is, how do you help them learn?
original_text: So if you're going to hire a junior person, the key is, how do you help them learn? And I think if you don't know what you're doing as the founder or the leader, it's hard. You're not going to be able to help them yourself. So you've got to be willing to invest in advisors like me, outside education, mentorship, coaching, otherwise, what's going to happen is that very driven, hungry and enthusiastic person is going to run through a lot of brick walls, which is great, except they're going to miss the fact that the door was standing right next to the wall that they just ran through and you're going to end up with a lot of bricks on the ground.

vocabulary.definition: An individual who establishes or originates a business or organization, often taking on a significant role in its early development and direction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startups, 'founder' refers to the person or people who create the company, often responsible for its vision, culture, and initial operations.
vocabulary.nuance: The term carries a sense of authority and responsibility, often implying a deep personal investment in the success of the venture.

text: I actually think if you're doing it right, sometimes conversion should actually decrease a little bit.
speaker: Adam Fishman
context: Lenny asks Adam how to think about onboarding as a conversion opportunity versus retention opportunity. Adam explains a counterintuitive principle: good onboarding optimization might actually reduce conversion rates slightly. He argues this is beneficial because it filters out unqualified users who would likely churn anyway, resulting in higher quality users who are more likely to retain and succeed with the product.
text_ko: 사실 저는 제대로 하고 있다면 때로는 전환율(conversion rate)이 오히려 조금 낮아지는 게 맞다고 생각해요.
text_zh: 我觉得如果你做对了的话，转化率有时候其实应该稍微降一点。
text_es: En realidad, creo que si lo estás haciendo bien, a veces las conversiones deberían bajar un poco.
key_sentence: sometimes conversion should actually decrease a little bit.
original_text: I actually think if you're doing it right, sometimes conversion should actually decrease a little bit. So you might actually have fewer people getting all the way through successfully, but I think that's okay because a lot of those people were probably not the right people for your product, which means they wouldn't have been engaged customers, they probably would have churned.

vocabulary.definition: The process of changing or transforming something into a different state or form, often referring to turning prospects into customers.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and marketing, conversion typically refers to the percentage of visitors to a website who complete a desired action, such as making a purchase or signing up for a newsletter.
vocabulary.nuance: While a high conversion rate is generally desirable, it can sometimes indicate a lack of quality engagement if achieved through aggressive tactics.

text: When you're interviewing at a company, you are actually investing an even more scarce resource. You're investing your time. There is no way to get more time. We're all on a finite clock. You can always get more money.
speaker: Adam Fishman
context: Lenny asks for tips on evaluating whether people at a company are a good fit before joining. Adam draws an analogy between job hunting and investing, explaining that candidates should do as much diligence as investors do when evaluating companies. He emphasizes that when you join a company, you're investing your most precious resource - time - which unlike money, can never be recovered once lost.
text_ko: 회사 면접을 볼 때는 사실 더 귀한 자원을 투자하는 거예요. 그건 바로 시간이에요. 시간을 더 만들어낼 방법은 없어요. 우리 모두에게는 한정된 시간이 있어요. 돈은 언제든 더 벌 수 있어요.
text_zh: 你去公司面试的时候，其实你投入的是更珍贵的资源——你的时间。时间是没办法再多要的，我们每个人的时间都是有限的。但钱嘛，总还是能想办法再赚的。
text_es: Cuando estás en una entrevista de trabajo, en realidad estás invirtiendo un recurso aún más escaso. Estás invirtiendo tu tiempo. No hay manera de conseguir más tiempo. Todos tenemos los días contados. Dinero siempre puedes conseguir más.
key_sentence: Interviewing is investing an even more scarce resource: your time, which is fleeting.
original_text: When you're interviewing at a company, you are actually investing an even more scarce resource. You're investing your time. There is no way to get more time. We're all on a finite clock. You can always get more money. If you make a bad investment decision, 'Okay, we lost there.' Provided you didn't bankrupt yourself. Even if you did, you can climb out of bankruptcy. There are things that you can do, but time is fleeting.

vocabulary.definition: The act of allocating resources, usually money, with the expectation of generating an income or profit. It involves taking calculated risks to achieve financial growth or returns.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, investing often refers to the allocation of capital into projects, stocks, or startups with the hope of increasing value over time. It is a fundamental concept in finance and entrepreneurship.
vocabulary.nuance: While investing typically implies a financial context, it can also refer to time or effort spent on activities that yield future benefits.

vocabulary.definition: Having limits or bounds; not infinite. It refers to resources or time that are limited in quantity or duration.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding that resources such as time, capital, and human talent are finite is crucial for effective planning and decision-making.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often carries a sense of urgency or scarcity, emphasizing the need for careful management of limited resources.

vocabulary.definition: A source of supply or support that can be drawn upon when needed, including financial, human, or material assets. Resources are essential for achieving business objectives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, resources can refer to anything from financial capital to human skills and technological tools that organizations utilize to operate and grow.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply both tangible and intangible assets, and its effective management is key to organizational success.
